title: Anaphylaxis
blurb: Spot a life-threatening allergic reaction fast, give IM adrenaline at the right dose and get help on the way.
question: A few minutes after the dentist puts on new gloves and places rubber dam, a patient says her lips are tingling. Within a minute her voice is hoarse, she is wheezing and a red rash is spreading up her neck. What is happening, and which drug must not be delayed?

teach.body: Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening allergic reaction. It comes on suddenly, gets worse fast and causes problems with the Airway, Breathing or Circulation, usually with skin or mouth changes such as a rash or swelling. It can follow a trigger within seconds or minutes and can kill within minutes. In the dental surgery the classic triggers are latex (gloves, rubber dam), medicines such as antibiotics, and chlorhexidine.

teach.caption: Skin signs alone suggest a mild reaction. Any Airway, Breathing or Circulation problem after a trigger means anaphylaxis.

teach.h: Triggers to watch for in the surgery

rows.label: Latex gloves, rubber dam, some equipment

teach.note: This is why the medical history asks about allergies at every visit, and why a latex-allergic patient needs a latex-free appointment.

steps.label: Recognise and shout for help
steps.sub: Stop treatment; remove the trigger (e.g. latex gloves, dam)

steps.label: Position
steps.sub: Lie flat, legs raised; sit up if breathing is difficult

steps.label: IM adrenaline 1:1000
steps.sub: Anterolateral middle third of the thigh

steps.label: Repeat adrenaline after 5 min
steps.sub: If no improvement; CPR if the heart stops

teach.h: Adrenaline 1:1000 (1 mg/mL) IM dose by age
head: Age
Dose
Volume
teach.caption: Resuscitation Council UK. Practices stock 1 mL ampoules or 0.5 mL prefilled syringes; a patient's own auto-injector can also be used.

teach.h: Why adrenaline, and why the thigh
teach.body: Adrenaline reverses what anaphylaxis is doing: it tightens leaky blood vessels to raise the blood pressure, relaxes the airway muscles to open the airways, and reduces swelling. Injected into the outer middle third of the thigh muscle, it is absorbed quickly and reliably, and it can go through clothing. 1:1000 means 1 mg in 1 mL, so the adult dose of 500 micrograms is 0.5 mL. Antihistamines act too slowly and do not treat airway or circulation problems.

teach.caption: If there is still no improvement after two doses, paramedics and hospital teams follow the refractory anaphylaxis pathway.

teach.text: Don't reach for the antihistamine or 'wait and see'. Antihistamine is only for a mild reaction with skin signs. Any Airway, Breathing or Circulation problem after a trigger means IM adrenaline now. Adrenaline in the dental surgery is always given into the muscle, never into a vein.

teach.body: Even if the patient recovers after one dose, they must go to hospital by ambulance, because symptoms can come back hours later. Write down the time and dose of every injection and hand this to the paramedics. Afterwards the dentist records the allergy clearly in the notes, a suspected drug reaction can be reported to the MHRA through the Yellow Card scheme, and future visits are planned around the trigger.

items: Anaphylaxis = sudden Airway, Breathing or Circulation problems, usually with rash or swelling, after a trigger.
Dental triggers: latex, antibiotics, NSAIDs, chlorhexidine.
Call 999, lie flat (sit up if breathless), IM adrenaline 1:1000 into the outer thigh.
Adult and over 12: 500 µg (0.5 mL). 6–12 yrs: 300 µg. 6 months–6 yrs: 150 µg. Under 6 months: 100–150 µg.
Repeat after 5 minutes if no improvement; high-flow oxygen; always to hospital.

summary: You can now tell a mild allergic reaction from anaphylaxis, name the dental triggers, lead the immediate response, and give IM adrenaline 1:1000 at the right dose for any age, repeating it after 5 minutes if there is no improvement.

A.q: Shortly after rubber dam is placed, a patient develops swollen lips, a hoarse voice and wheeze, and a rash on her neck. What is the most likely cause?
A.why: Sudden airway swelling, wheeze and rash after exposure to a trigger such as latex are classic signs of anaphylaxis.

whyNot.0: A faint causes pallor, sweating and brief loss of consciousness, not lip swelling or wheeze.
whyNot.1: Hyperventilation causes fast breathing and tingling, not swelling, hoarseness or a rash.
whyNot.3: Angina causes central chest pain, not allergic swelling or a rash.

A.q: What dose of adrenaline 1:1000 should be given intramuscularly to an adult in anaphylaxis?
A.why: Adults and children over 12 receive 500 micrograms, which is 0.5 mL of 1:1000 (1 mg/mL) adrenaline.

whyNot.1: 300 micrograms is the dose for a child aged 6 to 12.
whyNot.2: 150 micrograms is the dose for a child aged 6 months to 6 years.
whyNot.3: 1 mg (a whole 1 mL ampoule) is double the correct IM dose.

A.q: Where should intramuscular adrenaline be injected in anaphylaxis?
options: Into a vein in the hand
A.why: The anterolateral (outer) middle third of the thigh gives fast, reliable absorption and can be reached through clothing.

whyNot.0: Under the tongue is the route for GTN spray, not adrenaline.
whyNot.1: IV adrenaline is for specialists only; in the dental surgery it is given IM.
whyNot.2: The buttock is slower and less reliable, and the patient would need to be turned.

B.q: An 8-year-old develops anaphylaxis after an antibiotic. What dose of adrenaline 1:1000 IM is correct?
B.why: Children aged 6 to 12 receive 300 micrograms (0.3 mL) of adrenaline 1:1000 IM.

whyNot.0: 150 micrograms is for children aged 6 months to 6 years.
whyNot.1: 500 micrograms is for adults and children over 12.
whyNot.2: 100 micrograms sits in the range for babies under 6 months.

B.q: Five minutes after the first dose of IM adrenaline, the patient is still wheezy and pale. What should happen next?
options: Sit the patient up and wait
Give GTN spray under the tongue
B.why: If there is no improvement, the IM adrenaline dose is repeated after 5 minutes while waiting for the ambulance.

whyNot.0: Antihistamine is too slow and does not treat airway or circulation problems.
whyNot.2: Waiting without treatment lets anaphylaxis progress; the dose should be repeated.
whyNot.3: GTN treats angina and would lower the blood pressure further.

B.q: Which statement about anaphylaxis is NOT correct?
options: It can follow exposure to latex
It can cause a hoarse voice and wheeze
B.why: IM adrenaline is the first-line drug. Antihistamine is only used for mild reactions with skin signs.

whyNot.0: This is correct: latex in gloves and rubber dam is a recognised dental trigger.
whyNot.2: This is correct: a hoarse voice suggests airway swelling and wheeze shows breathing is affected.
whyNot.3: This is correct: in the dental surgery adrenaline is always given IM.

C.q: A patient with anaphylaxis is breathing comfortably but feels faint and very pale. How should they be positioned?
C.why: Lying flat with the legs raised helps the circulation when the blood pressure is falling. Sit them up only if breathing is difficult.

whyNot.1: Sitting up is for patients whose main problem is breathing; it can worsen a falling blood pressure.
whyNot.2: Standing or walking a patient in anaphylaxis can cause collapse.
whyNot.3: Lying face down makes the airway and breathing hard to monitor.

C.why: 1:1000 means 1 gram in 1000 mL, which is the same as 1 mg in 1 mL. So 0.5 mL contains 500 micrograms.

whyNot.0: 1 mg in 10 mL is 1:10,000, a weaker strength not used IM in the dental kit.
whyNot.1: 10 mg in 1 mL would be ten times stronger than 1:1000.
whyNot.3: 1 microgram in 1 mL would be a thousand times weaker than 1:1000.

C.q: After one dose of adrenaline, a patient's breathing and colour return to normal. What should happen now?
options: Finish the treatment once they feel well
Let them go home with a relative
Transfer them to hospital by ambulance
C.why: Everyone who has had anaphylaxis goes to hospital, because symptoms can return hours later even after a good response.

whyNot.0: Dental treatment must not continue after anaphylaxis; the patient needs hospital assessment.
whyNot.1: Going home is unsafe because the reaction can come back.
whyNot.3: Rebooking ignores the need for hospital care today.

reteach.title: The body's alarm, and the override switch
reteach.question: Think of anaphylaxis as every alarm in the body going off at once. What is going wrong, and how does adrenaline switch it off?

blocks.body: In anaphylaxis the immune system wildly overreacts to something harmless, like latex. It floods the body with chemicals that make blood vessels leak and widen, so the blood pressure falls and tissues swell, and it makes the airways tighten. Adrenaline is the body's own 'fight or flight' hormone. Given as an injection, it acts as the override switch, reversing each problem within minutes.

blocks.text: The adrenaline dose depends on age, not on how bad the reaction looks: 500 / 300 / 150 / 100–150 micrograms. If one dose hasn't worked after 5 minutes, give another.

explain.body: Anaphylaxis is sudden. Look for an Airway problem (swollen lips or tongue, hoarse voice), a Breathing problem (wheeze, breathlessness) or a Circulation problem (pale, clammy, faint, collapse), usually with a rash or swelling, after a trigger.

letters.sub: Swollen tongue or throat, hoarse voice

test.q: Which finding, together with a rash, tells you an allergic reaction has become anaphylaxis?
options: Mild redness at a glove site
test.why: A hoarse voice means the airway is swelling, which makes this anaphylaxis rather than a mild skin reaction.

whyNot.0: Itching is a skin sign and fits a mild reaction.
whyNot.2: Watery eyes are common in mild allergy and don't show ABC compromise.
whyNot.3: Local redness is a skin-only sign.

explain.body: Stop treatment and shout for help. Remove the trigger if you can, such as swapping latex gloves or taking out the dam. Call 999 and say 'anaphylaxis'. Lie the patient flat with legs raised, or sit them up if breathing is the main problem.

steps.label: Position
steps.sub: Flat, legs up (or sit up if breathless)

test.q: A latex-allergic patient reacts after the dentist forgets to change gloves. Which action comes first, alongside calling for help?
test.why: Removing the trigger stops further exposure while the team calls 999 and prepares adrenaline.

whyNot.0: Antihistamine is not the treatment for anaphylaxis.
whyNot.3: The history can be checked later; the patient needs action now.

explain.body: Adrenaline 1:1000 (1 mg/mL) is given IM into the outer middle third of the thigh. The dose is set by age band.

test.q: A 4-year-old has anaphylaxis in the waiting room. What dose of adrenaline 1:1000 IM is correct?
test.why: Children from 6 months to 6 years receive 150 micrograms (0.15 mL).

whyNot.1: 300 micrograms is for children aged 6 to 12.
whyNot.2: 500 micrograms is for adults and children over 12.
whyNot.3: 50 micrograms is not a recognised IM dose for any age band.

explain.body: Give high-flow oxygen and keep checking ABCDE. If there's no improvement after 5 minutes, repeat the adrenaline. If the patient stops breathing normally, start CPR. Record every dose and time, and make sure the patient goes to hospital.

test.q: How long after the first IM adrenaline dose can it be repeated if there is no improvement?
test.why: Resuscitation Council UK advises repeating IM adrenaline after 5 minutes if the patient hasn't improved.

whyNot.0: One minute is too soon for the first dose to take effect.
whyNot.1: Waiting 15 minutes would leave a deteriorating patient untreated.
whyNot.2: Thirty minutes is far too long in a life-threatening emergency.
